Forecasting Arbitrarily Linked Futures Streams with PCA, ARIMA, and Weak-Form Integration

Christopher M. Struck

Introduction

Bluntly, this project produced extremely modest forecasting gains. I cycled through different approaches to finding what I call a reference curve (and in more formal mathematical terms, I have called omni-dimensional equilibrium) before applying integration. After training a curve on futures data, I tested that reference curve on held out data to forecast different time horizons. Most forecasting attempts failed to beat carrying forward the last price badly, but since this curve and integration method had worked on physics data, I took a more mathematically fundamentalist approach. The task was to first find the best approach for the reference curve. Ultimately, after applying integration to the best reference curve, the combined method improved forecasts at several horizons.

In the physical examples that motivated this study, the form of a governing equation supplied a reference curve. This process worked immediately in the physical examples, because the equations were known and the system behavior was relative (not arbitrary). This study starts with five futures price histories and leaves the pattern of potential links unspecified. There was no guarantee that there would be a shared reference behavior. In this study, arbitrarily linked means that any connections may be indirect or reflect exposure to shared macroeconomic factors. A reference curve matters because it is the behavior of in this case the futures stream in the shared dynamical system. The combined result of reference and integration forecasts a price and defines the departure whose slope we try to explain.

ARIMA gave the study an optimal way to estimate and extend a candidate curve from observations. The early run fit each market separately. After principal component analysis (PCA) represented part of the variation as one shared movement, ARIMA could forecast that movement and translate it back into five distinct price paths. The experiments compared these paths and simpler references with carry-forward, the last observed settlement projected at every horizon. Many trial references produced higher price error than this baseline, so the study kept testing reference designs before evaluating their corrections.

The correction adapts the weak-form method described in Nonlinear Calculus in Practice: The Matrix of Error and Cross-System Integration (Struck, 2026). It tests whether shared movements in peer markets explain part of the slope of a departure from the reference. Integration by parts estimates signed contributions over short intervals from completed forecasts. The final approach shared here allowed linear and signed-square terms for each market pair, then integrated the retained rate adjustments back into prices. Controlled examples verified recovery of known terms. The futures results measure how well those estimated corrections transferred to later settlements.

Main Findings

The 90-session MA(1) with weak-form integration had the lowest average price error across the four horizons among the corrected configurations in the Stage 7 order grid. It beat every uncorrected setting in the grid at 30, 60, and 90 days. Carry-forward had slightly lower next-session error.

We evaluated 361 ARIMA candidates, each defined by an order and a training window. Each candidate received a separate accuracy score at four forecast horizons. The 90-session MA(1) with weak-form integration had the lowest average price error among the corrected candidates in the 2023 comparison. It also beat the best uncorrected ARIMA at each of the three longer horizons.

The corrected MA(1) forecast correctly called the direction of the price change from issue to target in 49.76%, 50.08%, and 51.20% of individual market forecasts at 30, 60, and 90 days, respectively.

A better forecast level in one case

In the 90-session MA(1) example, the raw paths had higher error than carry-forward at the three longer horizons. The correction reversed that result. The paths reached their final levels by trading session nine.

Stage 7 · 2023 issues

The broader experiment used completed 2022 outcomes to select ARIMA orders and then scored 250 issues from 2023. Keeping these scores separate preserves the shared-date historical comparison. Stage 6 Part 2 first used these 2023 dates for a fresh test, so the Stage 7 evidence is developmental.

Across 24 matched Stage 1–6 comparisons, the complete forecast beat carry-forward in 1. That was Stage 6 at 30 days, by 0.0011 percentage points of mean price error.

The reference beat carry-forward in 3 of 24 comparisons. The correction improved its own reference in 7. At 90 days, Stage 2 added 7.67 points of error to its ARIMA reference. Stage 3 recovered 5.61 points from a poor starting line. Stage 5 already had 200.50% error in the reference.

What the forecast diagnostics found

These diagnostics use the archived Stage 1–6 forecast results. They describe how the issued forecasts behaved. The PCA used to generate Stage 6 and 7 forecasts is shown separately in the stage tabs.

PCA of forecast outcomes

The first two components explained 71.3% of variation in the five standardized forecast-result features. The largest absolute weights were reference move size for PC1 and excess correction error for PC2. The analysis covers all 12,582 archived panel forecasts and uses realized outcomes. Stage 6 uses a separate PCA on past price changes to generate forecasts.

Data and evaluation

The five markets are VIX futures interpolated to 60 days and second-delivery-month settlements for WTI crude, Henry Hub natural gas, RBOB gasoline, and New York Harbor heating oil. The 2023 issues use settlements through March 28, 2024 for their longer targets.

Price accuracy uses mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). Each market receives equal weight. A positive gain is a reduction in MAPE versus carry-forward, stated in percentage points (pp). Wins, ties, and losses compare individual issues.

At a rolling cutoff, each lookback advances by one trading session and the model issues a new set of paths. The next-session target is one Cboe Futures Exchange session ahead. The longer targets are the first eligible sessions on or after 30, 60, and 90 calendar days. Shared dates are scored against the same realized settlements.

Across Stages 1–6, the tested corrections reduced held-out price error relative to their own references in 7 of 24 matched stage-by-horizon comparisons. The estimates came from integration by parts or from fitting the integrated correction directly to price departures.

  4. U.S. Energy Information Administration. Daily futures settlement histories, Contract 2. WTI crude oil · Henry Hub natural gas · RBOB gasoline · New York Harbor heating oil.

Stage 1 · Matched historical paths

The representative correction raised error at all four horizons. An early 2020 case got all five directions right with the market-specific reference, while forecasting much smaller moves.

Matched prior episodes across the futures, then issued market-specific paths or a shared pattern with signed market responses.

Stage 2 · ARIMA reference

ARIMA alone tracked carry-forward closely. The representative direct price-fit correction increased price error at all four horizons.

Stage 2 fit ARIMA separately to each market. It tested weak-form integration and direct fitting to price departures as two ways to estimate a correction to the same forecast paths.

Matched Stage 2 scores and selected orders

Stage 2 selected each market’s ARIMA order using 2018 data. It refit parameters every 21 trading sessions and updated the correction daily. Gasoline and heating oil selected ARIMA(0,1,0) without drift, which forecasts the issue settlement at every lead.

Across the original 60 panel-size, year and horizon comparisons, ARIMA and carry-forward differed by at most 0.02857 percentage points of average price error. The integrated-price correction beat both in 2 comparisons, both at the next session in 2022. The weak-form correction beat both in 0.

Stage 3 · Anchored regression lines

The representative correction cut 90-day error by 5.61 percentage points relative to its line. The corrected forecast still trailed carry-forward.

Fitted one line per future through its issue settlement and compared own-history and joint-history corrections.

Stage 4 · Daily joint reference search

With a planted missing contribution, the weak form improved all 12 synthetic target panels. It left all 12 sufficient reference panels unchanged. The representative futures setting trailed carry-forward at every horizon.

Searched for lagged interactions and refit 19 training windows daily. Paired blind tests isolated when a correction was needed.

At the next cutoff, a rolling window drops its oldest observation, admits the newest settlement, and issues another path. The lines in the chart are separate forecast vintages. Each path is evaluated from its own issue date.

Stage 5 · Anchored joint dynamics

The reference became unstable at longer leads. On the common 90-day cohort, reference error reached 200.50%.

Started the jointly fitted paths at the issue settlements and tested how the estimated rate equations behaved when projected forward.

Stage 6 · PCA-led dynamics

The shared reference achieved small gains at several horizons. Neither correction variant beat carry-forward across all four horizons at any one window in Part 2.

Forecast standardized changes in a smaller factor system with limited persistence. Part 2 kept one factor and refit all 19 windows on fresh 2023 dates.

2020–2022 reference comparison and June sensitivity

The Stage 6 PCA configuration selected in development used 80 training sessions, three PCA components and a correction fitted directly to price departures. On the narrower six-stage cohort, its reference gained 0.0063 points at 30 days and the correction added 0.0052 points of error. The full forecast’s gains by year were +0.0111 in 2020, -0.0071 in 2021, -0.0027 in 2022 percentage points.

Stage 6 originally scored 726 dates at 30 days and reported +0.0014 points of gain. The configurations below surfaced after scoring that wider grid. Their small pooled gains are exploratory. The paired fixture separately recovered a planted coefficient of −0.32 and preserved an already-sufficient reference.

All four retrospective configurations that beat carry-forward at every pooled horizon used one component. The 90- and 120-session references already did so without a correction.

Did the 110-session weak-form gain recur?

At 90 days, the 110-session weak form changed 3 of 250 forecasts. Against its own PCA reference it recorded 2 wins, 247 ties, and 1 loss. Mean price-error gain was -0.00097 percentage points against its own reference and -0.00122 against carry-forward.

The signed-square, three-session-lagged VIX-to-Henry-Hub term from June 2022 was selected 0 times across the fresh grid.

Stage 7 · PCA–ARIMA and joint corrections

The 90-session MA(1) with weak-form integration had the lowest average price error across the four horizons among the corrected configurations in the Stage 7 order grid.

Stage 7 scored the uncorrected ARIMA reference forecasts to establish how those paths performed on their own. It then tested weak-form integration against the same paths for orders selected using completed 2022 outcomes within each training window and differencing group.

Uncorrected ARIMA reference search

The reference search fit 19 ARIMA orders across 19 training windows and refit each of the 361 settings daily. Each setting received one average price-error score at each of four forecast horizons, across the same 250 daily issue dates and five markets.

The resulting 1,444 scores describe the uncorrected ARIMA search. Of those scores, 314 had lower average price error than carry-forward.

Stage 7 uses the same 250 issue dates at every horizon, from the 2023 block already examined in Stage 6 Part 2. Settlements through early 2024 complete the longer targets. Treat these as development results.

These bars show uncorrected ARIMA forecasts. The second number in each order is the number of additional differences on the PCA factor. Positive bars show lower average price error than carry-forward.

What carried forward from Stage 4

Stage 4 Part 3 chose a 35-session joint reference using completed 2019 outcomes. Its later 2020–2022 grid found small pooled gains at all four horizons with the 90-session joint reference. Stage 7 retained both windows within the full grid. Each day created a new forecast using that day's last 35–180 sessions and the same next-session, 30-, 60-, and 90-day target rules.

The wider run used 188 completed 2022 issues to choose one order within each training window and differencing group. ARIMA(0,0,1) was selected in 17 of 19 windows without extra differencing. The order stayed fixed for 2023 and its coefficients were refit every day. Both versions used all 19 windows.

How the 90-session MA(1) entered the test

Choosing one order for each window in each of the two differencing groups produced 38 reference configurations for the integration test. The 2022 scores selected ARIMA(0,0,1), or MA(1), for the 90-session window without extra differencing. Each selected reference was then scored before and after correction against the same 2023 settlements.

What weak-form integration added

The corrected 90-session MA(1) ranked first among the corrected configurations in 2023 when each of the four horizons received equal weight. At 30, 60, and 90 days, adding integration brought its average price error below that of the best uncorrected setting in the grid.

In the 90-session window, the 2022-selected MA(1) with weak-form integration reduced price error against carry-forward by 0.049, 0.037, 0.049 percentage points at 30, 60 and 90 days, respectively. Its next-session error rose by 0.003 points.

Among the orders selected without extra differencing, weak-form integration lowered error against its own uncorrected curve in 19 of 76 window–horizon comparisons.

In the separate screened comparison, a 95-session screened PCA–ARIMA(1,0,1) reference and a 95-session rank-1 PCA reference with the joint weak-form correction each edged out carry-forward at all four horizons. These two settings emerged from inspecting the 2023 results.

In a controlled test, weak-form integration recovered both coefficients (+0.70 and −0.60) when two streams made distinguishable contributions to a third. When only their combined effect was identifiable, the calculation recovered the combined coefficient (+0.50).

See five directly issued ARIMA price paths

Stage 2 fit ARIMA separately to each future. Stage 7 forecast a shared PCA movement with ARIMA and translated it back into five price paths. The uncorrected 90-session MA(1) forecasts had higher average price error than carry-forward at 30, 60, and 90 days. With weak-form integration, they had lower error at all three horizons. The corrected paths reached their forecast price levels by the ninth trading session and held those levels through the rest of the forecast. The gains measure average price accuracy at the target dates. January issues drove the pooled advantage. Across February through December issues, carry-forward had lower error at all three horizons. The next test is whether those gains repeat on fresh dates.
